q: Does the paper's core-proteome size (1202 orthologs) and clade split hold up when the 17 assemblies are rebuilt from raw sequencing reads with a modern uniform pipeline (e.g., SPAdes + Prokka or Bakta), instead of relying on the deposited NCBI PGAP re-annotation?
basis: Both this replication and the paper draw all quantitative claims (CDS counts, core size, protein-L presence) from annotations that were produced by different pipelines (Prokka in the paper, PGAP here). CDS count already differs by 1 gene at the mean (1759 vs 1760), and the +7-gene core discrepancy (1209 vs 1202) is consistent with CD-HIT tolerating what ProteinOrtho would split. None of this touches the underlying reads.
next_steps: Pull all raw Illumina/PacBio reads from ENA/SRA for the 10 new isolates and 7 previously published F. magna genomes (mapped via the 17 GCA accessions). Reassemble uniformly with SPAdes 4.x (or unicycler for the hybrid ones), annotate all 17 with Bakta v1.9+ on identical HMM databases, then recompute (a) CDS counts, (b) fastANI matrix, (c) CD-HIT core at c=0.5,n=3 and (d) ProteinOrtho core at default params. Compare all four numbers to both the paper and this replication; a stable core proteome under all three annotation pipelines would be a much stronger claim than the current same-annotation reproduction.

q: Is 'Finegoldia nericia' actually a valid separate species under current genome-based taxonomy standards (dDDH >= 70% and ANI >= 95%), and if so why has it not been formally described in the eight years since the paper appeared?
basis: The paper's central biological claim is that a novel species has been hiding within F. magna, supported by an inter-clade ANI of 90.7% (well below the 95% species threshold). This replication confirmed the 90.67% boundary and confirmed that ATCC 53516 and CCUG 54800 --- both historically deposited as 'F. magna' --- fall on the novel-species side. But the name 'F. nericia' remains provisional; no NCBI taxonomy record or LPSN listing exists.
next_steps: Run TYGS (Type Strain Genome Server) on the 17 assemblies plus the now-available 168 GCA Finegoldia records to compute formal dDDH values against F. magna ATCC 29328 and get a species-boundary call. In parallel, run GTDB-Tk classify_wf against GTDB r220+ to see whether GTDB has independently split the genus. If dDDH < 70% and GTDB agrees, prepare a formal species description (16S + genome-based, per Chun et al. 2018 rules) and submit to IJSEM with a proposed type strain (e.g., ATCC 53516). Cross-check whether Brueggemann or Soederquist's groups have a pending description that stalled --- direct email inquiry is warranted before duplicate effort.

q: How conserved is the sortase-dependent Fmp1/Fmp2 pilus gene cluster at the level of gene order, gene content, and Fmp1 sequence variation across the two clades, and does the pilus contribute to the clade-level pathogenicity differences the paper hints at?
basis: The paper claims the pilus locus is conserved across all strains but also notes Fmp1 protein-sequence heterogeneity. This replication only confirmed sortase presence per genome (4-9 sortases each) and did NOT reconstruct the Fmp locus synteny --- a genuine hole flagged in section 7 of REPORT.md and section 4 of the LaTeX critique. PGAP labels many pilus proteins 'hypothetical protein,' capping annotation-based inference.
next_steps: For each of the 17 assemblies: (a) extract the F. magna ATCC 29328 Fmp1/Fmp2/sortase reference cluster (approx 15-20 kb window) from RefSeq; (b) tblastn each ORF against every strain assembly and pull the +/- 25 kb window around each hit; (c) run clinker or Easyfig to visualize synteny; (d) build a Fmp1 amino-acid phylogeny (MAFFT + IQ-TREE with model selection) and overlay it on the ANI-based species tree to test co-phylogeny. If Fmp1 variants segregate by clade, that is a testable candidate for the pathogenicity-difference hypothesis; correlate with any available clinical-source metadata for the 10 Swedish isolates.

q: Does the two-clade / 90.7% inter-clade ANI structure persist when the analysis is scaled from 17 genomes (2018) to the 168+ GCA Finegoldia assemblies now indexed at NCBI (2026), or does the expanded corpus reveal additional intermediate lineages that would collapse the neat binary split into a continuum?
basis: REPORT.md section 4.6 already notes that the corpus has grown roughly 10-fold since publication (17 -> 278 records, 168 primary GCA). The paper's binary-clade claim is inherently sample-size-limited; small pathogen genome sets commonly show apparently clean splits that dissolve when more isolates are added. This replication reproduced the 2-clade cut on 17 genomes but did not test whether the boundary survives at n=168.
next_steps: Download all 168 primary GCA Finegoldia assemblies via NCBI Datasets (approx 350 MB). Run fastANI all-vs-all (n=168 -> 28,224 pairs, roughly 10-20 min on a laptop). Cluster with (a) average-linkage at the empirical valley in the ANI distribution, (b) single-linkage at the 95% species threshold, and (c) SplitsTree NeighborNet to detect reticulate signals. Report: number of species-level clusters, ANI distribution histogram (does the 90.7% gap survive as a genuine bimodal valley?), and any newly discovered sub-lineages. If a third cluster emerges, cross-check its geographic and clinical distribution against isolate metadata --- this could be the paper's most impactful follow-on.

q: Why is protein L (immunoglobulin-light-chain binder) confined to only 2 of 17 strains (both in the nericia clade in this replication), and does its presence correlate with any clinical or ecological niche differences among strains?
basis: The paper's most striking heterogeneity finding is that protein L is present in only ~10% of isolates; this replication reproduced 11% (2/17) and further observed that both hits fall in the nericia clade (0/9 magna, 2/8 nericia). That within-clade rarity is a real, sharp, biologically interesting signal --- unlike the CAMP factor (100%, floor-effect risk) or SufA (100%, universal), protein L looks like a genuine mobile virulence-factor candidate. The paper did not investigate its genetic context.
next_steps: For the 2 protein-L-positive strains (identify them from evidence/vf_results.json --- likely two of {09T494, 12T272, 12T273, 12T306, ATCC 53516, CCUG 54800, T151023, T160124}): (a) extract the +/- 20 kb region around the protein-L gene from each assembly; (b) test whether it is flanked by mobile-element signatures (integrase, transposase, prophage) using PHASTER or IslandViewer; (c) blastn the flanking region against nr to detect horizontal-transfer partners; (d) if raw reads are available, check for tandem duplications or copy-number variation; (e) mine isolate metadata for clinical-source information (wound vs blood vs commensal --- if the two protein-L-positive isolates cluster to a distinct infection type, that is a publishable niche-specialization hypothesis).
